did_you_know.text: Did you know? Jeremiah describes a warning system for danger: a horn is blown in Tekoa and a signal fire is raised in Beth-haccerem to announce that disaster is approaching from the north.
Did you know? The enemies are portrayed as shepherds arriving with their flocks and pitching their tents around Jerusalem—a picture emphasizing the city’s encirclement and siege.
Did you know? The enemies are determined to attack Jerusalem both by day and by night. They lament the passing of the day and decide to continue the attack in the darkness.

Did you know? Jerusalem is compared to a well or spring that holds its waters. Just as water collects there, so wickedness and violence continue to well up from within the city and resound throughout it.
Did you know? The expression “their ears are uncircumcised” figuratively describes people who are unable or unwilling to listen to the word of the Lord, so that his word becomes a disgrace to them.

Did you know? The people’s prophets are described as healing the nation’s wounds “superficially” and proclaiming, “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace. This depicts a false promise instead of genuine correction.

Did you know? The Lord tells the people to stop at the crossroads, ask about the “ancient paths,” and choose the good way, which leads to rest for their souls. But the people reply that they are unwilling to walk in it.

Did you know? Even frankincense from Sheba, fragrant cane from a distant land, and sacrifices are unacceptable to the Lord when the people’s actions are wrong. The chapter emphasizes that worship cannot replace moral conduct.

Did you know? The enemy who is about to come is described as a great nation from the north, armed with bow and spear, riding horses, and showing no mercy. News of them causes the people of the land to lose courage and tremble with fear.

Did you know? Jeremiah is appointed as a “tester”—one who examines and tests the ways of his people. At the end of the chapter, the people are compared to rejected silver, because even refining cannot remove their wickedness.
